literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's literature news is rich in voices, from liars and invalids to a painter's widow, and there's a good deal of prize talk and a little horror to finish.

Let me begin with narrators, since I know they're your first love. The Guardian reviews Attention Seeking Behaviour, a debut by Aea Varfis-van Warmelo that has been shortlisted for the Goldsmiths Prize. Its narrator shares the author's name and confesses, almost at once, that she is a liar. The reviewer calls it a slippery liar's tale, and sets it alongside Lolita and Atonement, two of the great books about storytellers who cannot quite be trusted. The questions underneath are memory, justice and truth: who gets believed, and why. If you ever want a modern companion piece for an unreliable-narrator unit, this sounds like one to look at.

The Guardian also reviews Hanif Kureishi's Are You With Me Now?, written after an accident left him tetraplegic. You might expect a subdued book, but the reviewer describes a novelist unleashed. The restrictions of his life, it seems, have given his narration a fresh and thrilling immediacy, rebellious and vivid. It's a striking thought, that a narrowed world can sharpen a voice rather than dim it.

Now to painting and writing, where two items meet nicely. The New York Times reviews The Widow van Gogh, a new biography by Joan Martelli. Its argument is that Vincent van Gogh's work might never have reached the world at all without his sister-in-law, Johanna van Gogh-Bonger. So this is less a story of a lonely genius than of the patient, practical work of making a legacy, and of the person who decided that the paintings deserved to be seen. It's a book about history and art, and also about who gets to tell a life afterwards.

And from The Paris Review, a smaller pleasure. Their fall issue cover is Elizabeth Glaessner's painting Big Head. The editors note that the title teases a tiny figure painting a giant head, which is a rather lovely image for the relationship between an artist and the work that towers over them. It's a small example of a literary magazine choosing a painting as its face, and it might be worth a minute with your pupils as a prompt for describing an image.

Next, novels and history. The Korean outlet Asia Economy has a piece on the South African novelist Damon Galgut, under the headline "I wish I could write a love story free from history". I only have the headline and the outline to go on, but it reflects on that wish and on the questions his fiction leaves open. It's a neat way into the idea that, for some writers, history is not background but something that follows the characters into the bedroom. That sits close to what you value in novels that teach more than essays can.

Also on the theme of stepping into another culture through fiction, The Booker Prizes site offers a reading list of five books by Mexican authors, prompted by Day of the Dead, which falls on the second of November. I don't have the titles to hand, but the idea suits your taste: books that open a culture to the reader without needing any prior knowledge. With the festival only a few days away, it's a timely thing to browse, perhaps with a view to your classroom shelves.

On to prizes. Sarah Howe has won the Forward Prize for Best Collection with Foretokens, at a ceremony at London's Southbank Centre. The prize carries ten thousand pounds. The book draws together new parenthood, the death of her father and her mother's early life in Hong Kong, so it moves between beginnings and endings, and between places. Poetry that holds a family's history in that way often makes very good teaching material.

For the fiction prizes, BBC Radio 4's Open Book has an eleven-minute episode called Who will win The Booker Prize? Simon Savidge goes through the shortlist book by book, and says both who he thinks will win and who he believes should. It's brief, thoughtful and unshowy, which makes it a good listen for a walk or a coffee if you like to hear contemporary novels discussed one at a time.

Finally, a pair of items about literature leaving the page. The Guardian reviews a new audio version of Bram Stoker's Dracula, directed by Mary Lambert and adapted by Robyn Aherne, with a starry cast that includes Jonathan Bailey. The reviewer admires the streamlined storytelling and an immersive, nightmarish sound design, calling it cinematic horror. Dracula is a book built from letters, diaries and voices, so it makes sense that it would thrive as sound. With Halloween just around the corner, this feels well timed, and since you enjoy a good thriller it might suit a dark evening.

And Local News Matters, in its Hooked on Books series, has a piece on George Saunders moving from page to stage in an opera style. All I have is the headline, so I can't say more than that, but given how musical Saunders' prose can be, the idea feels natural.

That's the shelf for today, Yamuna; I hope something on it keeps you company over the weekend.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's literary news is rich in voices: liars, invalids, widows and vampires, with a few paintings and a prize or two along the way.

Let me begin with narrators, since I know how much you love them. The Guardian has reviewed Attention Seeking Behaviour, a debut by Aea Varfis-van Warmelo, which has been shortlisted for the Goldsmiths Prize. The book's central trick is a bold one. The narrator shares the author's name, and she confesses, early on, that she is a liar. That is a wonderful provocation for a reader, because from that moment you cannot quite trust anything you are told, and yet you are asked to keep listening. The Guardian calls it a slippery liar's tale, and the reviewer sets it beside two famous books you will know very well: Lolita and Atonement. Both are novels in which a narrator's account of events, and the beauty of the telling, is part of the question of whether we should believe it. According to the review, this new book is concerned with memory, justice and truth, and with how a story can be told to shape what others think of us. I can imagine it being a lovely companion for a conversation with première students about unreliable narration, because the device is announced openly rather than slowly uncovered.

Another voice, quite different, comes from Hanif Kureishi. The Guardian reviews his new book, Are You With Me Now?, which he wrote after a devastating accident left him tetraplegic. The reviewer describes a novelist unleashed, and the central observation is intriguing. You might expect a restricted life to narrow the writing, but the reviewer finds the opposite: that the limits on his physical world give the narration a new and thrilling immediacy. The words used are rebellious and vivid. There is something moving in the idea that a writer, deprived of so much, finds that the sentence itself becomes more urgent. It is a reminder that style is not decoration, but a way of being present in the world, and sometimes the only way.

Now, to painting, where I have two items that feel very much in your territory. The first is in The New York Times, which reviews a new biography of Vincent van Gogh by Joan Martelli, called The Widow van Gogh. The title tells you where the emphasis lies. The book argues that Vincent's work might never have reached the world without his sister-in-law, Johanna van Gogh-Bonger. We tend to tell the van Gogh story as one of solitary genius, the single figure in the yellow room, the cornfield and the crows. This biography turns the camera round to look at the person who kept the paintings, believed in them, and did the patient work of making a legacy. It is a story about how art survives, about who decides what gets remembered, and about a woman whose labour sits behind one of the most famous reputations in painting. There is a good lesson in it, too, about how history is carried by people we rarely name.

The second is smaller, but charming. The Paris Review has unveiled the cover of its fall issue: a painting by Elizabeth Glaessner called Big Head. The editors note that the title teases something about the picture, which shows a tiny figure painting a giant head. I like the idea very much. A small person working away at an enormous face is almost a parable of how writers and painters feel: tiny against what they are trying to make. It is also a nice example of a literary magazine choosing a painting as its public face, which seems a good prompt, perhaps, if you ever want pupils to think about how an image can introduce a piece of writing before a single word is read.

From there, let me turn to history and the ways novels carry it. The Korean outlet Asia Economy has a piece on the South African novelist Damon Galgut, under the headline, in translation, "I wish I could write a love story free from history." The piece reflects on that wish, and on the questions his fiction leaves unanswered. I only have the headline and that brief summary, so I cannot tell you more of what he says. But the sentence itself is worth turning over. A love story, you might think, ought to be the most private thing a novel can offer, two people and nothing else. And yet here is a writer from South Africa saying he longs to write one free from history, which suggests that for him, and perhaps for many novelists, history keeps walking into the room whether invited or not. It is exactly the sort of idea that explains why novels teach the past so well: because the past will not stay out of people's private lives.

In a related spirit, The Booker Prizes has published a reading list of five books by Mexican authors, prompted by the Day of the Dead, which falls on the second of November. I do not have the titles in front of me, so I cannot name them, but the idea is a lovely one. The list is offered as a way into Mexican writing, and for a reader who likes to step into a story without needing to know the culture first, that seems a gentle and generous invitation. The Day of the Dead is, after all, a festival that holds memory, family and the dead close to the living, which is a very literary preoccupation. If you are thinking of something to read over the long weekend, this might be a good place to start browsing.

On to prizes, and a piece of good news from poetry. Sarah Howe has won the Forward Prize for Best Collection, for her book Foretokens. The Guardian reports that the book is about new parenthood, about her father's death, and about her mother's early life in Hong Kong. That is a striking weave: a baby arriving, a father leaving, and a mother's earlier world reaching back across geography and time. The prize was announced at the Southbank Centre in London, and it carries ten thousand pounds. I find it heartening when a collection built from family and grief and inheritance is recognised in this way. Poetry so often does the work of holding those three things together, birth, death and the stories our parents did not tell until later, and it is good to see a book like this celebrated.

Staying with prizes, but in a lighter, more conversational key, BBC Radio 4's Open Book has an eleven-minute episode called Who Will Win The Booker Prize? In it, Simon Savidge goes through the shortlist book by book. He says who he thinks will win, and, which is the more interesting question, who he feels should. That distinction between prediction and preference is where the best prize talk always lives. It is a short listen, ideal for a coffee or a walk down from Les Adrets, and it has the pleasure of thoughtful, unhurried discussion about contemporary fiction, without any of the shouting that can surround literary prizes.

Finally, let me end with sound and stage, two places where books are currently being taken off the page. The Guardian reviews a new audio version of Bram Stoker's Dracula, directed by Mary Lambert and adapted by Robyn Aherne, with a starry cast that includes Jonathan Bailey. The reviewer calls it cinematic horror with an A-list cast, praising the streamlined story and an immersive, nightmarish sound design. It is an interesting thing, an old gothic novel recast as pure listening, where the dark has to be built from voices, footsteps and atmosphere alone. With Halloween upon us, it feels well timed, and it might suit a long autumn evening with the lights low and the wind coming off Belledonne.

And last, a short note from the United States. Local News Matters, in its Hooked on Books series, has a piece headlined, "George Saunders wanders from page to stage, opera style." I should be honest that all I have is the headline, so I cannot say what the production is or where it is being staged. But I know you enjoy Saunders's prose, and I know you enjoy music, so the thought of his work meeting opera is a pleasing one. His writing already has a musical sense of voice and rhythm, and it is easy to imagine why it might want to be sung.

So, a liar who tells us she lies, a writer whose body is still but whose sentences are not, a widow who saved a painter, and a tiny figure painting a giant head. That seems like enough to be going on with. I hope the day treats you kindly, and that you find a good book, or a good sound, to keep you company.

art.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Friday the thirtieth of October, and today's art news pulls together a few things close to home, a pair of Lyon shows worth planning around, and some good stories where painting, music and fiction meet.

Let's start nearby. In Pontcharra, down in the Grésivaudan and hardly a stone's throw from Les Adrets, the local arts group Art'M is celebrating its twenty-fifth anniversary with an exhibition. Le Dauphiné Libéré says it runs until the sixth of November, so you have just over a week. A quarter of a century is a long time for a community arts association to keep going, and it's the sort of show that tends to feel warm and personal.

In Grenoble itself, Unidivers reports that the Mois de la Photo has taken the idea of hors-champ as its central theme. That's the off-frame, everything that sits just outside the edge of the picture. It's a lovely notion for a literature teacher, since it's close to what a narrator does when choosing what to leave unsaid. The report gives no dates or venues, so you'll need to look those up, but the theme alone is worth keeping in mind. And at the Musée de Grenoble, on Saturday the fourteenth of November, from ten until five, there's a day called Memento Vivere, exploring new imaginaries of death. The listing is brief, but the title is a nice twist on the old memento mori tradition, one that painters from the still life onwards would have recognised.

If you're thinking of a trip to Lyon, there are two good reasons. Le Petit Bulletin has reviewed the eighteenth Lyon Biennale, themed around the idea of passage, and calls it a very beautiful one. It praises a strong focus on Oceanian artists and the more intimate works, particularly at the Musée d'art contemporain. The same paper also points to Animal culte at the Musée des Confluences, an exhibition on how humans have related to animals across time and cultures. It moves from animal icons and companions to the mass decline of animal life, and it's the kind of show where history and anthropology do the storytelling together.

Now to the stage, where there are two items that I think you'll enjoy. The Guardian has a rave review of William Kentridge's Oh to Believe in Another World, staged in Baku. It's an hour-long collage animation, accompanied live by an orchestra playing Shostakovich's Tenth Symphony. The reviewer calls it an animated ballet of black comic pain, blending puppetry, dance and humour around grief and idealism. Kentridge pairing his drawn, flickering images with Shostakovich is a combination that seems made for your tastes, music with a shadow over it, and humour used to carry something heavy.

On BBC Radio 4, the Front Row programme looks at Nina Raine's six-hour adaptation of Middlemarch for the Royal Shakespeare Company. The review asks the question every reader of George Eliot will ask, which is how a stage version holds up against the novel. Six hours is a serious commitment, but then so is Middlemarch. The same episode also covers a British Library exhibition on Agatha Christie, marking fifty years since her death. A mix of Eliot and Christie in one programme feels like a good evening's conversation.

Two stories this week turn to photography, and to the people behind it. The Guardian profiles the Iranian-born artist Hoda Afshar, whose youth under Iran's morality police shapes her work, which finds humanity within inhumane systems. She says, and I quote, "I don't take freedom of speech for granted." The piece calls her work beautiful and shocking, and it leans on personal testimony and visual storytelling, so there's a strong narrator's voice behind the images.

The Guardian also has a gallery from the Deutsche Börse photography prize shortlist, which marks its thirtieth anniversary. The nominees look at hidden human labour, at life in wartime Ukraine, and at the Buddhist idea of rebirth. As a quick visual essay on what contemporary photography is doing, it's a good one to scroll through with a coffee.

And to finish, something for the pocket. The Guardian has rounded up four great exhibitions you can see for free. The headline promises skulls, bulls and, rather memorably, someone peeing in her own eye. Among them are Andy Warhol's skulls and Pierre Bonnard's fruit, which the writer argues have more in common than you might expect. Warhol and Bonnard side by side, one thinking about death and the other about ripeness, is a pairing that echoes quite neatly with that Memento Vivere day in Grenoble.

That's the picture for today, Yamuna, so enjoy your coffee and whichever of these frames catches your eye.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. This morning's briefing begins close to home, in Pontcharra and Grenoble, then goes down to Lyon, and ends with stage, page and photography from further afield, with a few things that might suit a free afternoon.

Let me start in the valley. In Pontcharra, the group Art'M is celebrating its twenty-fifth anniversary with an exhibition, and Le Dauphiné Libéré says you can see it until the sixth of November. That gives you about a week. Pontcharra is not far from Les Adrets, down in the Grésivaudan, so it is the sort of outing that fits easily into a Saturday morning, perhaps combined with a market. There is something I always like about the anniversary of a local arts group. Twenty-five years is a long time for people to keep making and showing work together, often without much fanfare, and an exhibition like this is usually a small portrait of a community as much as a display of pictures. I have no details here about what is on the walls, but the occasion itself is the story, and it is a warm one.

In Grenoble itself, the Mois de la Photo has arrived with a theme that I find rather beautiful: hors-champ, the off-frame, the thing that lies just outside the edge of the picture. Unidivers reports that the festival is putting this idea at the centre. The piece gives no dates or venues, so I can't tell you where to go, but the idea is worth turning over anyway. Every photograph is a decision about what to leave out, and the best ones make you feel the presence of what has been excluded, the way a good narrator can make you feel what they are refusing to say. You might even use it with your première students as a way into unreliable narration: what is the story's off-frame? It would be worth checking the festival's programme this week for the venues.

Also in Grenoble, the Musée de Grenoble is holding a day called Memento Vivere, with the subtitle "new imaginaries of death?", on Saturday the fourteenth of November, from ten in the morning until five in the afternoon. The listing is brief, so I can't say who is speaking or what form the day takes. But the title is a lovely inversion of the old memento mori, remember that you must die, turned into remember to live. Art and literature have always been the places where a culture works out how it feels about mortality, from the Dutch still life with its skull to the great elegiac novels. It's a Saturday, it's in the city, and it might be worth putting in the diary now.

Now to Lyon, where there are two things worth knowing about. The first is the Lyon Biennale of contemporary art, the eighteenth edition, which Le Petit Bulletin Grenoble reviews under the heading "un très beau passage", a very beautiful passage. The theme is passage, and the reviewer praises two things in particular. One is a strong focus on artists from Oceania, which is a part of the world that rarely gets this much room in a major European show. The other is the presence of more intimate works, especially at the Musée d'art contemporain. That second point appeals to me. Biennales can be exhausting, vast and loud, so a review that says the quiet pieces are the ones that stay with you is a useful guide if you are planning a day trip. Passage is a good word for a literature teacher too: the passage from one place to another, from one life to another, and of course a passage in a text. It would make a pleasing title for a lesson on journey narratives, if you were looking for one.

The second Lyon story is at the Musée des Confluences, where an exhibition called Animal culte looks at the relationship between humans and animals across time and across cultures. Le Petit Bulletin describes it as running from animal icons, the creatures people have worshipped or turned into symbols, through the animals we live alongside as companions, to the mass decline of animal life in our own time. The subtitle, roughly "our friends that we damage", gives you the tone: affectionate but not comfortable. It mixes history, anthropology and museum display, so it is the kind of exhibition where you learn how people have thought as much as what they have made. I could imagine it sitting beside a reading of any number of novels where an animal carries the moral weight, but I'll leave you to choose which. Since the Confluences and the Biennale are both in Lyon, they could make a single, rather rich day.

Let me move now to photography from further afield, since it ties in with that off-frame theme in Grenoble. The Guardian has a profile of the Iranian-born artist Hoda Afshar, under the headline that she does not take freedom of speech for granted. She grew up under Iran's morality police, and that experience shapes her work, which looks for humanity inside systems that are inhumane. The piece calls her work beautiful and shocking, and what stands out is how much it rests on personal testimony and visual storytelling. In other words, she is a kind of narrator, a person who has lived in a place and insists on telling it from the inside. If you enjoy strong voices on the page, this is a strong voice in images, and the profile is worth reading for that reason.

The Guardian also has a gallery from the shortlist of the Deutsche Börse photography prize, which is marking its thirtieth anniversary. The nominees explore hidden human labour, life in wartime Ukraine, and the Buddhist idea of rebirth. That is a striking range: the unseen work that keeps the world turning, a country at war, and the notion that endings are not final. Again there is a kind of off-frame at work, with the labour that goes unnoticed and the lives behind the headlines. The gallery is described as a good visual essay on contemporary photography, which makes it an easy and rewarding ten minutes with a coffee, and perhaps a good source of images to put in front of students for a discussion of how a picture tells a story.

Now to the stage, and to literature, which I know is closest to your heart. BBC Radio 4's Front Row has an episode that reviews two things you may well enjoy. The first is Nina Raine's adaptation of Middlemarch for the Royal Shakespeare Company, which runs to six hours. Six hours, for a novel that is itself a vast, patient study of a whole community. The programme asks how the stage version compares with the book, which is the question every lover of the novel will want answered: what survives the journey from page to stage, and what changes? George Eliot's great gift is her narrator, that wise, ironic voice that moves between characters and comments on them, and it is fascinating to wonder how a theatre company handles that without a narrator on the page. I can't tell you what the reviewers concluded, but the question alone is good listening, and if you teach any adaptation work, it is rich ground.

The same episode covers an exhibition at the British Library on Agatha Christie, marking fifty years since her death. For a reader who loves a thriller, this is a pleasing pairing with Eliot, one the great Victorian novel of provincial life and the other the great architect of the puzzle. I only have the outline, that it marks the anniversary of her death, but libraries are good places for this sort of show, because they can set out manuscripts and the writer's working life. Front Row also reviews a film called Gentle Monster, but I know that is less your territory, so I'll simply mention that it is there.

From the page back to the stage, and to something quite extraordinary. The Guardian reviews William Kentridge's Oh to Believe in Another World, which was staged in Baku. It is an hour-long animation made from collage, and it is accompanied by a live orchestra playing Shostakovich's Tenth Symphony. The reviewer calls it an amazing animated ballet of black comic pain. Kentridge brings together puppetry, dance and humour, and the subjects are grief and idealism, which is to say the ache of believing in a better world and the loss that follows. Shostakovich is a perfect partner for that, since his music so often holds sorrow and irony in the same breath. The title itself, "Oh to believe in another world", is almost a line of poetry. You love dance, classical music and inventive art, and this brings all three together, so it is the sort of thing to keep an eye out for if it travels. Kentridge is also an artist whose work teaches history better than a textbook, because he makes the weight of it felt, and that is something I think you appreciate in fiction.

Finally, something to enjoy without opening your purse. The Guardian has a roundup of four great free exhibitions, under a headline that mentions skulls, bulls and someone peeing in her own eye, which I admit made me smile. Two of them are named in the piece I have: Andy Warhol's skulls and Pierre Bonnard's fruit. The writer argues that the two have more in common than you might expect, and I like that. A skull and a bowl of fruit are both old subjects in still life, both quietly about time passing, and each artist handles them in a very different way. It is a lovely echo, in fact, of that Memento Vivere day in Grenoble, which asks similar questions about mortality in a different register. These are British shows, so they are not for a casual weekend, but the pairing is a good thing to bring into a lesson on how painting and writing return to the same themes.

So that is the week: a local anniversary in Pontcharra before the sixth of November, Grenoble thinking about the off-frame and about death, Lyon offering a Biennale of passage and a museum full of animals, and further afield a great photographer, a great novel on stage and a ballet of paper and music. I hope something here tempts you out into the valley, or at least to a comfortable chair with the radio on.

Enjoy the day, Yamuna, and may it be full of beautiful passages.

around.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It is Friday the thirtieth of October, and the valley and Grenoble are heading into the Toussaint weekend with a pleasing mix of stories, screens and exhibitions.

Let me start with something happening today, because it is rather charming. At the Bibliothèque in Sainte-Marie-d'Alloix, in the Grésivaudan, there is a storytelling show called Kamishibike, from eleven o'clock until noon. It uses kamishibai, the Japanese picture-card theatre, where the storyteller slides illustrated cards into a little wooden frame and tells the tale as each image appears. Here it is done by bike, which sounds wonderfully inventive. It is exactly the sort of story you can step into without needing to know anything beforehand, so if your morning is free and you fancy a gentle outing, it is well worth knowing about.

Now, a theme I suspect will please you: documentaries. Le Dauphiné Libéré reports that the Mois du film documentaire, the national documentary film month, is coming to the Grésivaudan valley. Alongside that, the Grésivaudan's own agenda lists a month of documentary screenings in the libraries across the valley. I have to be honest that neither piece gives me dates, titles or venues. The details sit on the Grésivaudan listing page, so it would be worth a look there, especially if you are hoping for something on music or dance, though I cannot promise that from what I have in front of me. Libraries are a lovely place to watch a film, and the screenings are close to home.

Turning to Grenoble, the Toussaint weekend is well supplied. The site jds.fr has published a roundup of nine outings for the weekend, from today until Sunday the first of November. Among them is a fair of creative workshops, which could be fun if you like making things with your hands. I only have the headline, so I cannot tell you what the other eight are, but the article should give you a quick overview if you are looking for ideas.

Several shows in Grenoble began yesterday and run until Sunday the first of November. One is called "On a échangé nos ados", which translates roughly as "We swapped our teenagers". It is described as a cultural show, and from the title I would guess it is a comic or thoughtful look at adolescence and family life. That is a subject you know rather well from the classroom, though I have no further detail about the format or the venue. Running over the same dates is another called "Charge mentale : sauve qui peut !", or "Mental load: every man for himself!". The listing is thin, but the title promises a lively, perhaps humorous look at the endless invisible to-do list of everyday life. Both are listed through Isère Attractivité, so their pages should give you times and places if either catches your fancy.

If you would rather linger over something quieter, there are three exhibitions to know about. The first is a free exhibition in Grenoble on the Groupe militaire de haute montagne, the army's mountain unit. It opened on the seventh of February and runs right to the thirty-first of December, so there is no rush. Given how close the high Alps are to your doorstep, it should be an interesting piece of local history, the human side of those peaks that you see from the Grésivaudan.

The second, also free and in Grenoble, is a travelling exhibition called Métamorphoses urbaines, put together by IUGA, about the transformations of the city. It runs from the eighth of September to the thirteenth of November. If you enjoy seeing how a place changes over time, and how a city carries its past in its streets, this one has a deadline in a fortnight or so, so it is the one to prioritise.

The third is in Montbonnot-Saint-Martin, where the Grésivaudan artothèque is showing works from its collection. An artothèque is a lending library for art, where people can borrow original pieces for their homes, so an exhibition is a nice chance to see what is on the shelves, so to speak. The summary gives no dates, so do check the Grésivaudan page before setting off. Montbonnot is also just a short hop along the valley from you.

Last, one item with a practical, community spirit. Economie Matin reports around one hundred events in Grenoble devoted to repairing things and consuming differently, repair cafés among them. It gives no dates in the text I have, but it is a good sign of how much of this sort of local, hands-on activity goes on in the metropolis, and a good place to take a broken lamp or a stubborn zip if you have one lurking at home.

So, to sum up: a bicycle storytelling show this morning in Sainte-Marie-d'Alloix, a documentary month building in the valley's libraries, a busy Toussaint weekend of shows and workshops in Grenoble, and three exhibitions to pick from at your leisure. I hope you find a little time to wander through at least one of them, and that the autumn light over Belledonne is kind to you today.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Friday the thirtieth of October, the Toussaint weekend is just beginning, and the last couple of days have brought a pleasant handful of things happening around you, some of them today.

Let me start with the one that's today, because it's the most time-sensitive. This morning, Friday the thirtieth of October, from eleven o'clock until noon, there's a storytelling show at the Bibliothèque in Sainte-Marie-d'Alloix, in the Grésivaudan. It's called Kamishibike, and it's a performance of contes, tales, told with kamishibai, the picture-card theatre, and delivered by bike. Kamishibai, if you've not met it, is a way of telling a story by sliding illustrated cards through a little frame, so that the pictures and the voice work together. It's a form that doesn't ask anything of its audience beforehand. You simply sit down and the story comes to you, which is very much the kind of story you like, the kind you can step into without needing to know the culture first. The listing doesn't say who the performers are, or whether it's aimed at children or at a mixed audience, and it doesn't mention booking, so if you'd like to go, a quick call to the library this morning would be sensible. It's an hour, it's a morning, and it sounds like a gentle, inventive way to begin the holiday weekend.

Now to Grenoble, where a number of things are clustered around the Toussaint weekend, from the thirtieth of October to the first of November. The Grenoble outlet jds.fr has put together a roundup of nine outings for the weekend, and one of them is described as a fair of creative workshops, a Foire aux ateliers créatifs. I have to be honest that all I have is the headline, so I can't tell you what the other eight outings are, nor where the fair is held, nor what times. But a roundup of nine suggestions for three days is a useful thing to have open on your phone if the weather turns, or if you find yourself in the city with a free afternoon. Creative workshops, in particular, can be a nice thing to wander through, and if there's a stall or a demonstration involving books, paper, printing or drawing, it might well catch your eye. That's a guess, mind you, not something the listing says.

Also in Grenoble, and running from Thursday the twenty-ninth of October until Sunday the first of November, there are two cultural shows with rather appealing titles. The first is called On a échangé nos ados, "We swapped our teenagers". The listing gives no further detail, so I can't say whether it's theatre, comedy, a talk, or something in between. But the title suggests a piece about teenagers and, perhaps, about the adults who live alongside them, which is a theme you'll recognise from the classroom. Whether it's funny, tender or both, I don't know, but a title like that promises some observation of the real texture of adolescent life, which is where so many good narrators begin.

The second show, over the same dates in Grenoble, is called Charge mentale : sauve qui peut ! That is "Mental load: every man for himself", or perhaps more freely, "run for your life". Again the listing is thin, but the title points towards a lively, probably humorous look at the invisible mental load of organising everyday life: the lists, the reminders, the things that have to be remembered by someone. It's the sort of subject that lends itself to comic writing and sharp characters. If either of these two catches your interest, I'd suggest looking up the venue and the times before setting out, since I have only the dates and the city, and a show that runs across four days will not necessarily be on at every hour of every day.

Let me turn now to something that I think will appeal to you rather directly: documentaries. The Mois du film documentaire, the national documentary film month, is making its way into the Grésivaudan valley. Le Dauphiné Libéré reports on it, and the Grésivaudan's own agenda lists it as a month of documentary screenings in the valley's libraries. Unfortunately, neither of the pieces I have includes dates, venues or titles of films. The detail is on the page the listing links to, so it's worth a visit to the Grésivaudan libraries' website, or a word with your local bibliothèque, to see what's on and when. I mention it anyway because it's a rare thing to have a programme of documentaries come to you rather than the other way round, and because library screenings tend to be a quiet, unhurried way of watching a film, often with the chance to talk about it afterwards. I can't promise that part, since the listing doesn't say, but it's worth asking. You've said you enjoy documentaries about dance and classical music, and while I can't tell you whether any of the screenings touch on those subjects, the month is a good reason to look.

Next, exhibitions, of which there are three that you can plan around at leisure, which is rather lovely, since none of them is a rush.

The first is in Grenoble: a free exhibition on the Groupe militaire de haute montagne, the army's high-mountain unit. It opened on the seventh of February and runs all the way to the thirty-first of December this year, so you have two months left to go and see it, and no ticket to worry about. It's a piece of local history with a strong Alpine link, and for someone who lives on the slopes of Belledonne and looks out over the valley, it's a subject that sits close to home. I don't have the venue or the opening hours from the listing, so a quick check beforehand is wise. But with such a long run, you can choose a quiet weekday, or a grey afternoon when the mountains are hidden in cloud and you'd rather be indoors thinking about them.

The second is also in Grenoble and also free: a travelling exhibition called Métamorphoses urbaines, put on by IUGA, about the transformations of the city. It has been going since the eighth of September and ends on the thirteenth of November, so it's the one with the nearest deadline, a little over two weeks from now. It shows how Grenoble has changed over time, and it's the sort of exhibition that lets you look at a familiar place with fresh eyes. If you enjoy the way novels use a city as a character, with streets, neighbourhoods and buildings carrying the weight of history, you may well enjoy seeing a real city's changes laid out in the same spirit. Because it's a travelling exhibition, I'd check where in Grenoble it's currently installed before you go.

The third is a bit further along the valley, in Montbonnot-Saint-Martin, where the Grésivaudan artothèque is showing works from its collection. An artothèque, for anyone who hasn't used one, is a lending library for artworks: you can borrow pieces to hang at home, rather as you'd borrow a book. The listing says L'artothèque s'expose, "the artothèque is on show", but it doesn't give dates or hours, so do look at the page before planning a trip. Given your interest in the links between paintings and literature, it could be a pleasant place to browse, and I wonder whether a work you saw there might even find its way onto your wall for a few weeks. That's a daydream of mine, not something the listing promises, but the lending idea is real.

Finally, something a little different, but in keeping with local life. Economie Matin reports on about a hundred events in Grenoble devoted to repairing things and consuming differently. Repair cafés are the example given, where people bring a broken lamp, a torn jacket or a stubborn toaster and someone helps them mend it. The report doesn't give dates or locations, so I can't tell you which of these fall over the coming weekend, but a hundred is a lot, and it suggests that there'll be something on in the weeks ahead. I know you tend to steer away from economics, so I'll say that I'm mentioning this not as a piece of economic news but as local colour: a community of people who like to mend and share, which has a certain charm of its own. If you ever have a book with a loosened spine or a favourite bag with a broken zip, it may be worth a look.

So, to gather it together. Today, there's Kamishibike in Sainte-Marie-d'Alloix from eleven until noon. Across the weekend, from today until Sunday, Grenoble has its nine Toussaint outings, plus the two shows, On a échangé nos ados and Charge mentale : sauve qui peut ! In the longer run, you've got the documentary month in the Grésivaudan libraries, the free mountain-unit exhibition in Grenoble until the end of the year, the free urban-transformations exhibition until the thirteenth of November, the artothèque show in Montbonnot-Saint-Martin, and the repair events scattered across Grenoble. For several of these, I only have a headline, so it's worth a quick look at the original pages for times and venues. But the overall picture is a gentle, varied start to the holiday, with stories, pictures, a bit of mountain history and plenty of choice.

Enjoy the weekend, Yamuna, and may the best story find you wherever you go.

bfi.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Friday the thirtieth of October, and today's BFI corner is mostly theatre: several of your set works on stage across Britain, and a sad piece of news about a great Shakespearean actor.

Let me begin with Twelfth Night, which turns up twice. Everything Theatre has published a review of a production at the Crucible Theatre. The piece I have is brief, so I can't tell you much about the staging itself, but a critical account of a recent production is always handy for the 2027 session, whether you're working with seconde or planning ahead for première and terminale. Reading it alongside your own text might prompt a good question for students: what does a reviewer notice about tone, pace and casting that a reader on the page might miss?

The second Twelfth Night item is from the Taunton Daily Gazette, which reports a reimagining of the play as a 1960s jazz club. I only have the headline, so I can't say who is behind it or where it's playing. But the idea is rich enough to use on its own. A jazz club is a world of music, disguise, late nights and a little melancholy, and that suits a play that opens with "If music be the food of love". You could ask students to imagine their own setting for the play and justify it with lines from the text. It's a neat way into adaptation, and it works whatever the level.

Staying with Shakespeare, The Reviews Hub has a review of Space Hamlet at the Cockpit in London, a stage reworking of Hamlet. The text I have is short, but the premise speaks for itself. Moving Elsinore into space is a bold act of interpretation, and it invites the question of what is essential in the play. Is it the court, the ghost, the delay, the language? For première students especially, that could make a lively discussion or a short creative task: relocate Hamlet, and defend what you keep.

From Shakespeare to Dylan Thomas. Swansea Bay News offers a reviewer's verdict on Swansea Little Theatre's Under Milk Wood at the Dylan Thomas Theatre. The headline asks whether it's worth seeing, so the piece is a judgement on the staging. Under Milk Wood is a play for voices, and of all your works it is perhaps the most naturally musical, so any review that comments on how a company handles the sound of Thomas's language is worth a look. Even if Swansea is a long way from Les Adrets, a review like this can help you decide what to listen for when you play students a recording or a clip.

There's also a Sheridan link, though a slightly indirect one. The Northwich Guardian reports that a theatre in the town will stage a wartime comedy, Jack Absolute Flies Again, from this November. The title suggests a nod to Jack Absolute, the dashing young man in The Rivals, which is on the 2027 programme. I don't have more detail, so I wouldn't want to claim exactly how the two are connected. But if the connection is as the title implies, it's a nice example of a later writer borrowing a famous character from the eighteenth century and carrying him somewhere new. Students might enjoy guessing what a character like Jack would be up to in wartime before you tell them anything more.

Now the sadder news. The Guardian reports the death of Sir Patrick Stewart at the age of eighty-six, describing him as a Star Trek actor and an acclaimed thespian. Several other outlets have followed with tributes. CP24 has a profile covering his life from nineteen forty to twenty twenty-six, tracing his path from Shakespearean actor to starship captain. The Irish News has a feature arguing that before Star Trek fame arrived, Shakespeare was his first love. And PBS has posted an In Memoriam on its Great Performances news page, which points to his stage and screen work and may be a useful starting point if you're looking for recordings to share with students.

For the classroom, I think the Irish News angle is the most appealing. Many students will know him only as the captain of a spaceship, and the idea that a classical stage actor became a household name for something quite different is a good hook. It could open a short discussion on what it means to perform Shakespeare, and how an actor's training in verse and voice shapes everything they do afterwards. If you do use a clip from any of the plays, even a brief one, it would make a fitting way to mark his passing. The Guardian's obituary is the most authoritative of these, so if you only read one, I'd choose that.

Finally, a piece of news about international sections. The mairie of the sixth arrondissement in Paris is hosting an exhibition marking twenty years of the Polish international section at the Lycée Montaigne. The information I have is thin, and Paris is some distance from Grenoble, so this is more of a curiosity than something you can visit. But it's a pleasant reminder that these sections have a history and a community around them, and that a twentieth anniversary is something worth celebrating. If your own section has a milestone coming up, it might be a model for how to mark it.

So the picture today is of Shakespeare, Thomas and Sheridan very much alive on British stages, with a gentle farewell to an actor who spent a lifetime with the language you teach.

Enjoy your Friday, Yamuna, and may the weekend bring a good book and a bit of sunshine over Belledonne.
bfi.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quieter couple of days for official BFI texts, but the stage has been busy with several of your 2027 works, and there is a sad piece of news for anyone who teaches Shakespeare.

Let me begin with the theatre, because four of the programme's plays have turned up in the last forty-eight hours, each in a slightly different guise. I should say at the outset that most of these items reached me as little more than a headline or a short summary. I'll tell you what is actually known, and where I'm offering a teaching thought of my own, I'll say so.

Twelfth Night comes up twice, which is fitting for a play that is all about doubles. First, Everything Theatre has published a review of a production at the Crucible Theatre. I don't have the review's content beyond the fact that it exists, so I can't tell you what the production did or how the critic judged it. But a full critical account of a staging of a set text is always worth a few minutes of your time. If it's a thoughtful review, it could become a short source text for première: students read a professional response to a performance, then write their own, arguing for or against the director's choices using quotations from the play.

The second Twelfth Night item is more intriguing. The Taunton Daily Gazette reports on a reimagining of the play as a 1960s jazz club. Again, all I have is the headline, so I can't tell you who is staging it or how far the idea is carried through. Still, the premise alone gives you plenty to work with. The play opens with music, with Orsino asking for more of it, and the idea of a world run on appetite, mood and improvisation sits quite naturally beside jazz. That is my thought rather than anything the report says, but it makes a good seconde discussion question: what does a change of period and setting bring out in a text, and what does it quietly cover over? You might ask students to pick one scene, say Malvolio's humiliation or the shipwreck and arrival, and describe how they would stage it in a jazz club, then justify each choice from the words on the page. It's a gentle way into the idea of adaptation without needing any special knowledge of the period.

The same adaptation question arises with Hamlet. The Reviews Hub has a review of Space Hamlet at the Cockpit in London, a stage reworking of Shakespeare's tragedy. Once more the text I have is short, so I can't say how the space setting works in practice. But there is a lovely line in the play for exactly this conversation. When Hamlet tells Rosencrantz and Guildenstern that he could be bounded in a nutshell and count himself a king of infinite space, were it not that he has bad dreams, he is already talking about confinement and vastness at once. Whether or not the production uses that line, it offers you a way of testing the idea with première: does setting Hamlet among the stars make his isolation more literal, and is that a gain or a loss? Students who find the play remote might enjoy being asked to defend or demolish the concept, as long as they ground their argument in the text.

From Shakespeare to Wales. Swansea Bay News has published a reviewer's verdict on Swansea Little Theatre's production of Under Milk Wood at the Dylan Thomas Theatre. The headline asks whether it is worth seeing, which suggests a fairly direct, readerly review, though I can't tell you the verdict itself. What I can say is that this is a play that belongs in the ear before the eye. It begins with a narrator inviting us to begin at the beginning, in a small town on a spring night, moonless and starless and bible-black, and the whole piece depends on voices drifting from house to house. That is language that begs to be read aloud, and I know that's what you enjoy most in a text. If you are planning a lesson, a nice approach would be to let students hear the opening before they see it on the page, then ask them to draw or describe what they imagined, and only afterwards to read the review and compare it with what a real company chose to do. The fact that this is a local amateur company in Dylan Thomas's own town gives the exercise a sense of place that students may find rather moving.

The last stage item connects to Sheridan. The Northwich Guardian reports that the town's theatre will stage a wartime comedy called Jack Absolute Flies Again, from November. The name suggests a link to Jack Absolute, the character in The Rivals, though the report as I have it doesn't spell out the connection, so I'd treat that as likely rather than confirmed. If it does build on Sheridan's character, it is a charming example of a later work borrowing a figure from an eighteenth-century comedy and carrying him into a different age. Even without knowing more, it prompts a good question for première: why do certain characters survive being lifted out of their original plays? Jack Absolute is a young man who adopts a false identity to win the woman he loves, and that sort of disguise travels well from one era to another. It is a reminder that The Rivals isn't just a museum piece but a play whose types still turn up on stage.

Now to the news that will have touched many people who love the theatre. The Guardian reports the death of Sir Patrick Stewart at the age of eighty-six. It describes him as a Star Trek actor and an acclaimed thespian, and that pairing of words says a good deal about the shape of his public life. It is the most authoritative of the notices I've seen, and as you'd expect it treats his stage reputation as seriously as his screen fame.

Three other outlets have marked his death, each with a different emphasis. CP24 carries a profile of his life, from nineteen forty to twenty twenty-six, which traces the journey in its headline from Shakespearean actor to starship captain. The piece appears to be brief, but the framing is useful, because it puts the theatre first, which is how he began. The Irish News goes further and argues that, before accepting Star Trek fame, his first love was Shakespeare. That is a lovely angle for a class, because it presents classical training not as a dusty qualification but as the foundation of a whole career, and a love that lasted long after the cameras arrived. And PBS has posted an In Memoriam tribute on its Great Performances news page. The text is thin, but the page points towards his stage and screen work, and Great Performances is the sort of place where you might find filmed theatre that could be shown in class. I wouldn't promise anything specific until you've looked, but it is worth a search.

How might you use all this with students? One gentle idea would be a short lesson on what it means to speak Shakespeare as an actor. Students could choose a speech from Hamlet or Twelfth Night and discuss how pauses, emphasis and breath change meaning, using the tributes as a starting point for the idea that an actor's life can be a lifelong conversation with a single writer. Many of your students will know him, if at all, from science fiction, which could be a good way in: the same voice, they might be surprised to learn, spent decades on the great Shakespearean roles. It may also be a quiet moment for older students to reflect on what a death means for the way we remember a performer, since performance is the one art that disappears as it happens, and recordings are all that is left.

Finally, a note for those of us who work in international sections. The mairie of Paris's sixth arrondissement is hosting an exhibition marking twenty years of the Polish international section at the Lycée Montaigne. The information I have is slim, and Paris is a good way from Grenoble, so it isn't something you could easily pop along to. But it is a reminder that these sections are communities with their own histories, and that twenty years is a real milestone. If your own British section has an anniversary approaching, or simply a story worth telling, the idea of an exhibition in a public building might be a lovely model: old class photographs, student writing, programmes from school productions. It could even connect with this week's theme, since a school performance of one of your set texts would make a fine item in such a display.

To gather the threads together: three of this week's productions are about adaptation, whether it's a jazz club, outer space or a wartime comedy, and the question underneath each is what a text can bear when you move it somewhere new. The fourth, Under Milk Wood in Swansea, offers the opposite lesson, which is that some writing needs very little except voices and a good ear. A small practical plan might be to choose one review, ask students to read it as a piece of argument, and have them write their own staging proposal in reply. Even where the reviews themselves are brief, the questions they raise are not.

That's all from the BFI corner for today, Yamuna, and I hope the weekend brings you a good book and a little of that Belledonne light.

good.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. The last two days have brought a pleasing mix of books, birds and small kindnesses, with a good deal for a lover of stories.

Let me begin with the page and the past. The New York Times has reviewed a new biography of Vincent van Gogh by Joan Martelli, called The Widow van Gogh. Its argument is that his work might never have reached the world at all without his sister-in-law, Johanna van Gogh-Bonger. It is a book about how a legacy gets made, and about the quiet person who does the making. That sits nicely beside a story in The Guardian about a cache of rare love letters written by La Pérouse, the scientist who was lost on Louis XVI's round-the-world voyage, which set sail in 1785. The letters were written to a French aristocrat, and they give a personal account of the expedition. It is an old maritime mystery seen through the eyes of a man in love, which is almost a novel already.

Also from The Guardian, some good news for poetry. Sarah Howe has won the Forward Prize for Best Collection, worth ten thousand pounds, for Foretokens. The book moves between new parenthood, the death of her father and her mother's early life in Hong Kong. The prize was announced at London's Southbank Centre. It sounds like a collection that holds the intimate and the historical in one hand, and it might be worth keeping in mind for your own shelves.

Staying with the past, Good News Network reports that researchers have replicated Roman dichroic glass, the kind that changes colour depending on the light, after around sixteen hundred years. Anyone who has seen a piece of it will know the effect: one colour when the light falls one way, another when it falls differently. It is a lovely meeting of ancient craft and modern materials science. And the same outlet's history column notes that on the thirtieth of October, 1973, the Bosporus Bridge was completed, joining mainland Europe to Anatolia for the first time. The piece dwells on the engineering, with its steel towers and inclined hangers.

Closer to home, Le Dauphiné Libéré tells us that in Pontcharra, down in the Grésivaudan not far from you, the arts group Art'M is celebrating its twenty-fifth anniversary with an exhibition. It runs until the sixth of November, so there is just about a week left. A quarter of a century of local creative life is worth marking, and it might make a pleasant outing.

Now to nature, where there are several encouraging stories. Positive News reports from Namibia, where rangers are combining smartphones and real-time data with traditional tracking skills. The aim is to help farmers and protect a recovering population of desert lions. What I like is that the old knowledge is not being replaced; it is working alongside the new tools, and both are doing their part.

On the water, Good News Network describes a device built by Princeton alumni that filters microplastics out of wastewater. It was inspired by water-repellent plants, and it is already in use in Atlantic City, stopping plastics before they reach the Atlantic. It is a concrete result rather than a promise, and that is always welcome.

The same outlet also has something for the mind. New research suggests that the expertise needed to identify birds helps preserve neuroplasticity, and may slow cognitive decline as we age. The article opens with Emily Dickinson's line about hope having feathers, which seems apt. So the next time you hear an unfamiliar song in the woods above Les Adrets, you may be doing your brain a favour by trying to put a name to the singer.

And for something lighter still, off the coast of Boston Bay in South Australia, a ship's captain spotted something odd in the water: a juvenile kangaroo, swimming more than a mile and a half out to sea. A scuba diver and his crew rescued it. Nobody seems quite sure what it was doing out there, but it is now safely back on dry land.

Two stories now about people. In Incheon, near Seoul, a stranger quietly paid a four hundred and twenty dollar barbecue lunch bill for twenty-seven people, staff and disabled residents of a community centre, and then left without being identified. Small, specific and generous.

And there is a character who could easily carry a film. Good News Network highlights a short documentary called Panther Pat, about Pat Palinkas, an elementary school teacher who in 1970 became the first woman to play professional football, taking the field for the Orlando Panthers. She has been nearly forgotten, and the film sets about putting that right. It sounds like the sort of story that makes a good case for a teacher as a hero.

Finally, two items from the world of education and film. Reasons to be Cheerful describes a student exchange scheme that never leaves the United States, built on the sociologist Saskia Sassen's idea that culture is not bounded by national borders. Students travel between very different parts of the same country and meet unfamiliar worlds there. As someone who works in an international school, you may find the idea interesting to turn over. Good News Network also introduces JoyDrops, a curated slate of short documentaries with positive outlooks, made by filmmakers already recognised on the festival circuit. The piece reads partly as promotion, but it may point you towards a few films worth seeking out.

That is the news for today, Yamuna, and I hope the day treats you as kindly as that stranger treated those twenty-seven lunch guests.
good.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It has been a gentle couple of days for good news, with a lovely thread running through it of things that last: letters, glass, bridges, poems, and the people who carry them forward.

Let me begin with the written word, since I suspect that is where you will want to linger. The New York Times has a review of a new biography by Joan Martelli, called The Widow van Gogh. Its argument is one you might enjoy putting to a class: that Vincent van Gogh's work might never have reached the world at all without his sister-in-law, Johanna van Gogh-Bonger. We tend to tell the van Gogh story as a story of one solitary man and his canvases. This book turns the lamp towards the person who inherited the paintings and the legacy and, as the review presents it, made the difference between obscurity and fame. It is a book about painting, about history, and about how a reputation is built by patient, unglamorous work. There is a good lesson in it for any of us who care about stories: sometimes the most important character is the one standing just outside the frame.

Staying with history that reads like fiction, The Guardian reports on the discovery of a cache of rare love letters written by La Pérouse. He was the scientist who was lost on Louis the Sixteenth's round-the-world voyage of seventeen eighty-five, one of those great maritime mysteries that has never quite let go of the French imagination. The letters were written to a French aristocrat, and they give a personal account of the expedition. So rather than the official record, the logbooks and the instructions from the court, we are offered the voice of a man writing from the inside of the adventure, with his heart as well as his instruments. For a teacher who loves history learned through narrators, that is rather perfect. One can almost hear the voice: a scientist, far from home, writing to someone he loves, not knowing what lies ahead of him. It is the sort of material from which a novelist could build a whole book, and it is real.

And then a piece of news for poetry lovers. Sarah Howe has won the Forward Prize for Best Collection for her book Foretokens. The prize was announced at London's Southbank Centre and carries ten thousand pounds. The collection is about new parenthood, about the death of her father, and about her mother's early life in Hong Kong. That is a remarkable triangle of subjects: a baby arriving, a father leaving, and a mother's earlier world, a place and a time before she was anyone's mother. It sounds like the kind of poetry that holds together beginnings and endings in the same breath. If you are looking for something musical and personal to read aloud in a quiet moment, it may be worth a look.

Now to the hands and minds that make things, across the centuries. Good News Network reports that researchers have replicated Roman dichroic glass, the kind that changes colour depending on the light, after roughly sixteen hundred years. If you have ever stood in front of an ancient glass vessel that glows one colour with the light behind it and another with the light in front, you will know the magic of it. For a long time it was a skill that had simply been lost, and now it has been recovered, a fine meeting of ancient craft and modern materials science. There is something moving about the idea that a craftsperson's secret, lost for sixteen centuries, can be coaxed back into the light, quite literally. I rather like it as a reminder that history is not only about kings and battles, but also about objects, and the ingenuity behind them.

The same outlet has a short history piece for today's date. On the thirtieth of October, nineteen seventy-three, the Bosporus Bridge was completed, linking mainland Europe with Anatolia for the first time. The piece highlights its engineering, including the steel towers and the inclined hangers that carry the deck. It is a nice image for a morning like this: two continents, brought together by a line of steel across a strait, fifty-three years ago today. Anyone who has read a novel set in Istanbul will know how much that city lives on the meeting of two worlds, and this bridge made that meeting something you could cross on a daily commute.

Now, to the natural world, where there are several cheerful stories. Positive News reports from Namibia, where rangers are combining real-time data and smartphones with traditional tracking skills. The aim is twofold: to help farmers and to protect a recovering population of desert lions. I love the way the story is framed. It is not technology replacing old knowledge, nor old knowledge resisting technology, but the two working side by side. A tracker who can read the ground, and a phone that tells the farmer where the lions are right now, are a better team than either alone. And the fact that the lion population is described as recovering is, in itself, good news worth pausing on. These are animals that live in some of the harshest country on earth, and here are people finding ways for farmers and lions to share the landscape.

Also from Good News Network, a story to make you smile, and perhaps a little to wince. Off Boston Bay in South Australia, the captain of a boat spotted something very odd in the water: a juvenile kangaroo, swimming more than a mile and a half out to sea. A scuba diver and his crew went to the rescue and brought the kangaroo to safety. It is hard to say which is more charming, the image of a young kangaroo paddling gamely away from the shore, or the sight of a diver turning up to help. It is the sort of story that needs no moral at all, only a little delight.

On a more serious environmental note, there is real progress against microplastics. Princeton alumni have built a device, inspired by the way certain plants repel water, that filters microplastics out of wastewater. It is already in use in Atlantic City, which means it is not just a promising prototype but something doing the work today, stopping plastics from reaching the Atlantic Ocean. I find the nature-inspired part especially satisfying. A leaf that sheds water has been doing quiet, elegant engineering for millions of years, and here are people paying attention to it. It is a concrete step, and concrete steps are what we are after in this briefing.

And one more from the natural world, which I saved because it begins with a line of poetry. Good News Network reports on new research suggesting that birdwatching may actually reshape the brain. The idea is that the expertise needed to identify birds, the fine attention to a flash of colour, a shape in flight, a snatch of song, helps preserve neuroplasticity and may slow cognitive decline as we age. The piece opens with Emily Dickinson's line that hope is the thing with feathers, which is a rather lovely way to begin an article about science. I think there is something in this for readers as much as for birdwatchers. Expert attention, practised over years, seems to be good for the mind, whether we are looking at a wren in a hedge or a sentence in a novel. Up in Les Adrets, with the valley below and the woods around, you are surely well placed to test the theory.

Let me turn now to people, and the small and large kindnesses they offer one another. In Incheon, near Seoul, a stranger anonymously paid a four-hundred-and-twenty-dollar barbecue lunch for twenty-seven people: staff and disabled residents of a community centre. That is the whole story, and it is a good one. There was no announcement and no credit taken, only a meal quietly paid for and a table of people who, presumably, had a very pleasant afternoon. Good news does not always have to be large to be real.

Good News Network also introduces a short documentary about Pat Palinkas, nicknamed Panther Pat. She was an elementary school teacher who, in nineteen seventy, became the first woman to play professional football, taking the field for the Orlando Panthers. She has been almost forgotten, and the film sets out to put that right. I think you will appreciate her as a character: a teacher, in a classroom by day, who walked onto a professional pitch and made history. It is the sort of story that works even if you know nothing about American football, because at its heart it is about someone doing something nobody expected of her.

Closer to home, and I hope a little treat for the weekend, Le Dauphiné Libéré reports that in Pontcharra, in the Grésivaudan valley not far from you, the arts group Art'M is celebrating its twenty-fifth anniversary with an exhibition. It runs until the sixth of November, so there is still a little time to go. A quarter of a century is a good long run for any local association, and it says something about the people who have kept it going, year after year, simply because they love making and sharing art. If you are looking for an outing between lessons, it could be a pleasant one.

From the world of education, Reasons to be Cheerful has an article on a student exchange scheme that never leaves the United States. It draws on the sociologist Saskia Sassen's idea that culture is not bounded by national borders. The thought, as I understand it, is that you can meet a very different culture without crossing an ocean, and that exchange can happen within a country as well as between countries. As a teacher at an international school, you will have views of your own on what mobility does for young people. It is an interesting counterpoint, a reminder that curiosity about other ways of living can be cultivated close to home, and that the borders that matter are not always the ones on the map.

And finally, Good News Network introduces JoyDrops, a curated slate of award-season documentary shorts with positive perspectives, made by filmmakers who are already recognised on the festival circuit. I should say that the piece reads as partly promotional, so take it with a pinch of salt. Still, it points to short films that might be worth seeking out when you want half an hour of something uplifting, and short documentaries are, after all, a lovely form for a quiet evening.

So there we are: letters from a lost voyage, a prize for poetry, lions and kangaroos and birdsong, and a stranger's kindly lunch. I hope the day treats you as gently as these stories treat their subjects, and that something on the way catches the light like a piece of Roman glass.
