france.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Friday the thirtieth of October, and this morning's France briefing is a gentle one, with a lost voyage, a few words about words, an orchestra in the thick of it, and the first shivers of Halloween.

Let me begin with the item I think you'll enjoy most, because it reads like the opening of a novel. The Guardian reports on a cache of rare love letters written by La Pérouse, the scientist who vanished on Louis XVI's round-the-world voyage, which set out in seventeen eighty-five. The letters were written to a French aristocrat, and they give us something the official record rarely does, a personal account of the expedition. Most of us know the outline of the story: a grand royal enterprise, a ship that sailed into the Pacific and never came home, and a mystery that has fascinated people ever since. What these letters seem to offer is the human voice inside that mystery. Not the log, not the report to the Crown, but a man writing to someone he loved, from a long way off, about what he was seeing and living through.

I find that is often how history lands best. You can teach the date and the cause, but it's the private voice that makes a student lean forward. And a lost expedition, a king on the eve of revolution, and letters that crossed oceans are almost too well-made for fiction. If you ever wanted a way into the late eighteenth century for a première class, a voice speaking across the distance of a voyage would be a lovely place to start. The Guardian's piece is the place to look for the detail, and it's worth saying that I only have the outline here, so I can't tell you what the letters actually say. But the idea alone, a mystery at sea told through love letters, is a gift.

From letters to language. The Local France has a piece with a rather mischievous headline, about a town in France where, apparently, locals speak "perfect" French. The text itself is quite thin, so I won't pretend to tell you which town it is or how the claim is made. But the question underneath it is a delightful one for a teacher of English living in France. What do we mean when we say someone speaks perfect French, or perfect English, for that matter? Every country has its town, or its region, or its radio presenter, said to speak the language in its purest form, and every such claim tends to say as much about how we think of standard language as it does about the people being praised. In Britain we've argued for generations about which accent counts as correct, and the argument is never really about vowels. A piece like this is a pleasant prompt for a lesson on regional speech and the idea of a standard, even if the article itself is light.

Staying with words, The Local's French Phrase of the Day is, fittingly for the week, "des bonbons ou un sort". That's the French version of trick or treat, literally "sweets or a spell". I rather like it. The English "trick" is a prank, a bit of mischief, while the French "un sort" is a spell or a curse, which sounds much more like something out of an old tale. It's a small thing, but it's the sort of tiny difference between two languages that makes translation so interesting, and it might make a nice minute at the start of a class this week, when the pupils' minds are no doubt drifting towards pumpkins anyway.

Now, a bit of music, and a bit of courage. The Guardian has a piece about L'Orchestre du Nouveau Monde, a Paris orchestra that drew attention last week by playing through tear gas during the student protests. That's quite an image: musicians, instruments in hand, carrying on while the air around them stings. The article places the group within a tradition of radical orchestras, ensembles that see themselves not as guardians of something sacred and untouchable but, in the words of the headline, as a tool for struggle. There's a real argument in that. We often think of the classical orchestra as the most formal, even the most conservative, of institutions, all black tie and polite applause. This piece asks what happens if you treat it instead as a living instrument that can go into the street. I'll leave the protest itself to one side, since that's the background here rather than the point, and I know it's not where your interest lies. But as a classical-music story, about what an orchestra is for and where it can play, it's a thought-provoking read, and it connects nicely to the documentaries about music and dance that I know you enjoy.

On a sadder note, the world of stage and screen has lost a great figure. Franceinfo reports that the British actor Patrick Stewart died on Wednesday, the twenty-eighth of October, at the age of eighty-six. The French headline quotes someone saying that he played so many mythical roles, and that captures it well. Many people will know him as Captain Picard in Star Trek, and as Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films. But his career ran for around sixty years, across both stage and screen, which is a reminder that behind the famous screen roles there was a long working life in the theatre. Franceinfo describes a wave of emotion at the news. For someone who teaches English, there's something fitting in remembering a British actor whose voice was so recognisable, and who is so closely tied in many minds to the idea of the commanding, thoughtful speaker. I only have the headline facts here, so I'll simply say that it feels like the end of an era for many people who grew up with those characters.

Now to the season. Halloween is almost upon us, and The Local has several pieces circling around it, each from a slightly different angle. The first asks why Brittany and Normandy have Samhain festivals. Samhain is the festival drawing on Celtic traditions and wider European folklore, and Halloween is often traced back to it. The piece is short, so it offers a glimpse rather than a deep history, but the link is intriguing: that in two regions of north-western France, the old autumn festival has its own marked place on the calendar. If you like the idea that stories and customs travel, change their names, and come back in new costumes, this is a nice small example. Brittany, with its Celtic heritage, is perhaps the less surprising of the two, but Normandy sitting alongside it is a good reminder of how layered the cultural map of France really is.

The Local's weekly La Belle Vie column then pairs two quite different pleasures: comforting French autumn food, and suggestions for what it calls terrifying Halloween nights. It's a light lifestyle roundup, pleasant rather than substantial, and I won't invent a menu for you. But I like the pairing. There's something very right about the idea of a warm, hearty dish in the evening followed by a good fright, and it fits the mood of this time of year in the mountains, when the days shorten and the cold starts to creep down from Belledonne. If you fancy something local and seasonal, it may be a good week for the producers' markets, though I'd check what's actually on before heading out.

Looking a little further ahead, The Local also has a preview of six things to look forward to in France in November. It frames them against a backdrop of colder weather and ongoing strikes, so it's honest that the month isn't all sunshine, but the piece is meant as a seasonal pick-me-up. I can't list the six for you, as I haven't got the detail, but it's a light guide that might well suggest cultural or local events worth noting in the diary. November, with its early dark and its low light, is often a good month for exhibitions and concerts, so it may be worth a look if you're planning some weekends around the Grésivaudan and Grenoble.

Since strikes have come up, a word of practical caution. The Local describes strikes as ongoing, so if you're travelling anywhere by train in the coming days, it would be wise to check the transport information for your specific route before setting off. I don't have details of which services are affected, so I'd rather not guess.

Now to La Mire, the daily round-up of French television, with two editions to mention. The edition for the twenty-ninth of October is, I'm afraid, mostly grim. It includes a train crash in Spain and debates on racism. But there are two brighter items, and they're rather lovely. One is about a postman who delivers the post by rowing boat, which is exactly the sort of gentle, slightly improbable local story that makes a morning feel better. I'd love to know where he rows and what the post looks like arriving by water, but I only have the headline, so I'll let your imagination do the work. The other is a segment titled "Romanin, l'autre Jean Moulin", the other Jean Moulin. Jean Moulin is, of course, one of the great names of the French Resistance, so the title suggests a lesser-known figure of the same period being brought into the light. I don't know more than that, but it's the kind of story that can teach history in a way a textbook paragraph can't, and may be worth watching for that segment alone.

The edition for the twenty-eighth of October is a television zapping round-up. It touches on the Israeli elections, on Mbappé finishing second in the Ballon d'Or, and on a government plan to restrict social networks. I'll leave the politics there. But the programme also asks a question that I suspect will resonate with a teacher: are we all addicted to screens? It's a question you probably see answered, in one way or another, in every classroom. It could easily become a discussion topic, or even a writing prompt, particularly with older pupils who have strong opinions about their phones. And if you think of the great narrators of fiction, many of them are people who looked up from whatever was in front of them and paid close attention to the world, which makes a nice counterpoint.

So, a gathering of small pleasures this morning: a lost voyage told through love letters, a question about what perfect French really means, an orchestra that plays on through the smoke, a farewell to a much-loved actor, and a postman in a rowing boat to remind us that not every story is heavy.

I hope your Friday is warm and unhurried, Yamuna, and that someone offers you a sweet before anyone casts a spell.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's a gentle day for watching, with a good deal of ballet after yesterday's World Ballet Day, some thoughtful reportage from Arte, and a few thrillers to keep an eye on.

Let me start with the dance, since the Royal Ballet has been busy. Its World Ballet Day livestream ran yesterday, the twenty-ninth of October, so the live event has passed, but a good number of the videos are still there to watch on YouTube. I should say plainly that YouTube is not one of your platforms, but everything here is free, so it costs you nothing to look.

The one I would put first is the Royal Ballet's introduction to Kenneth MacMillan's Manon. It is described as a devastating ballet, set in eighteenth-century Paris, about a woman torn between love and wealth. That is a strong character caught in a very human dilemma, and the introduction is a good way into the story before you ever see a full performance. It would also sit nicely beside any conversation about heroines who have to choose between the heart and survival.

Alongside it is a short rehearsal film from World Ballet Day, called Insight: Visionaries. It shows the dancers preparing Visionaries: Robbins and MacMillan for the main stage. There is something lovely about watching the work before it becomes polished, the repetition and the small corrections, when you know what it is all heading towards.

The third is the Royal Ballet's World Ballet Day video for this year, called How Stories Are Made. This version is the BSL one, with British Sign Language. It is about how stories take shape in the studio, and how knowledge passes from one generation to the next. It is a replay of the livestream material, so you can pick it up whenever you like.

That theme of handing things down comes up again in a fourth video, a short spotlight on the dancer Lauren Cuthbertson. She recalls learning the role of Juliet from Monica Mason, in MacMillan's Romeo and Juliet, and talks about the value of passing knowledge between generations. If you are teaching Shakespeare this year, there is something quietly touching about hearing a dancer describe inheriting Juliet, almost as a role handed over in a classroom.

Now to Arte, which has three pieces worth knowing about, all on its YouTube channel.

The most moving, I think, is an Arte Regards reportage from Valence. It follows young volunteers who are restoring photographs lost in the floods of October twenty twenty-four. More than a million images are still waiting to be saved. The film runs for thirty minutes and is available until twenty twenty-seven, so there is no rush. It is a story about memory, about what ordinary people choose to keep, and about the patience of people who care for the pictures of strangers. It is also close to home, in the Rhône valley region, which gives it extra weight.

The second is an episode of the Arte series PhantasIA, called La fabrique des émotions artificielles. It looks at how artificial intelligence is learning to recognise, imitate and govern human emotions. The episode ranges across acting, neurodivergence, psychiatry and facial recognition. It is a serious subject, but the range of angles suggests it is more human than technical. You might find it useful if your older pupils are thinking about what it means to write or perform feeling, and whether a machine can ever do it convincingly.

The third is lighter in tone. It is an Arte Twist episode asking why cute things do us so much good, from kawaii culture to Labubu keychains. It is presented as a thoughtful cultural piece that links art, design and our search for reassurance in troubled times. It is a nice little reflection, and probably a good one for a quiet evening.

Finally, the thrillers, and here I need to be honest that the details are thin. Three articles appeared, but each gave only a headline, so I can tell you what they promise but not much more.

First, Netflix. ScreenRant reports a new four-part thriller in which a dream getaway turns into a nightmare. It is due to premiere on the thirty-first of October, which is tomorrow, so it is worth checking the listing on Netflix for the exact date. Four episodes is a very manageable length, and the setup is the classic one of paradise going wrong.

Second, HBO Max. ScreenRant has a piece saying that HBO's eight-part psychological thriller has become a must-watch once again. The headline does not say which series it means, so I cannot tell you more, but HBO Max is one of your platforms, so it may be worth a look through the thriller section if you are in the mood for something tense.

Third, MovieWeb praises an eight-part mystery thriller by Harlan Coben as a gripping one-night binge, calling it his wildest. Again, the headline does not give the title, the plot or the platform. If you enjoy his twisty style, you might look up which of his adaptations is meant, but I would not want to guess.

So, to sum up. If you have time for only one thing, I would choose either the Manon introduction for pure storytelling, or the film about the Valence photographs for something with real heart. The thrillers can wait until the weekend, when we may know more.

Enjoy your day, Yamuna, and may your evening viewing be both beautiful and a little bit tense.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's the thirtieth of October, and today's watching has a little of everything: a thriller arriving tomorrow, a few good things from ARTE, and a cluster of Royal Ballet films left behind by World Ballet Day.

Let me begin with the thrillers, since one of them has a date attached. ScreenRant reports that Netflix has a new four-part thriller premiering on the thirty-first of October, tomorrow. The premise, as the headline puts it, is a dream getaway that turns into a nightmare. I should be honest that this is all we have: the piece is only a headline, so there's no title, no cast and no plot beyond that one line. The headline mentions a Friday, but the date it gives is the thirty-first, so do check the date on Netflix itself. What I can say is that four episodes is a very manageable length. It's the sort of thing one could watch over a single wet autumn weekend without it swallowing the whole of it. A holiday that goes wrong is also a classic set-up for the genre, because people are away from home, away from their usual certainties, and often stuck with companions they don't know as well as they thought. If that appeals, it's worth a look when it appears.

The second thriller is on one of your platforms too. ScreenRant has a piece about an eight-part psychological thriller from HBO, which it calls a masterpiece and says has become a must-watch once again. HBO Max is where you'd look. Again, the text we have is only a headline, so I can't tell you the title, the story or why it's returning to attention. I mention it mainly as a signal: a critic thinks an eight-part psychological thriller is worth revisiting, and if you spot a series on HBO Max described in those terms, it may well be the one. Eight episodes is a good length for psychological suspense, since it gives the characters room to unravel properly rather than just being hurried towards a twist.

The third is from MovieWeb, which praises a Harlan Coben eight-part mystery thriller as a gripping one-night binge, and calls it his wildest. Once more it's only a headline. The plot isn't given, and neither is the platform, so I can't say where to find it. But since you enjoy thrillers, the name may be enough to search for. A word of caution on the phrase "one-night binge": eight episodes in a single evening is a lot, and I'd treat it as a compliment to the pace rather than as advice. Perhaps two evenings, with a pot of tea, and a firm decision about when to stop.

So that's the thriller shelf: one with a firm date, and two worth keeping in mind until more detail turns up.

Now to the dance, which is where the richest material is this morning. The Royal Ballet and Opera held World Ballet Day on the twenty-ninth of October, and its livestream has now passed. But the company has left a good trail of films on YouTube. These aren't on any of your platforms, but they're free, and they suit your love of dance and of dramatic storytelling.

The first I'd point you to is an introduction from the Royal Ballet to Kenneth MacMillan's Manon. It's described as a devastating ballet, set in eighteenth-century Paris, about a woman torn between love and wealth. As a story, it has everything you like: a strong central character, a historical setting that one can step into without any specialist knowledge, and a dilemma that's both personal and social. A woman is pulled between what her heart wants and what the world offers her, and the ballet tells that story through movement rather than words. As someone who teaches narrators and characters, you might enjoy thinking about how a dancer shows a character's inner conflict with no voice at all. An introduction film is a good way to approach it: it sets out the story and the world of the piece before you ever see a full performance. I can't tell you from the description how long it is, or exactly who appears in it, but it's presented as an accessible starting point.

The second film is called World Ballet Day Insight: Visionaries. It's a short Royal Ballet video showing dancers in rehearsal as they prepare a programme called Visionaries: Robbins and MacMillan for the main stage. I like rehearsal films for a particular reason. A finished ballet looks effortless, almost inevitable, and a rehearsal shows the opposite: the repetition, the corrections, the slow building of something fragile. The title pairs two choreographers, Robbins and MacMillan, so the programme brings together two distinct storytelling voices. It's short, so it could be a very pleasant coffee-break watch.

Third is the Royal Ballet's World Ballet Day twenty twenty-six video, called How Stories Are Made. This one is listed as a British Sign Language version, so it has BSL interpretation. It looks at how stories are made, and at how knowledge passes from generation to generation in the studio. That idea of inheritance, of a craft handed down from person to person, is a thread that runs through several of these films, and I find it quite moving. It's a replay of the livestream material, so you can watch it at your own pace.

And that thread comes through most clearly in the fourth film, a spotlight on the dancer Lauren Cuthbertson. In it she recalls learning the role of Juliet from Monica Mason, in MacMillan's Romeo and Juliet, and she talks about the value of passing knowledge between generations. It's a lovely little portrait of how a part is not simply learned from a score but handed over, by someone who has lived inside it. For a literature teacher there's a parallel with the way a text is taught: not only the words on the page, but the way one reader hands their understanding to another. If you're looking for something to share with a class, perhaps in a lesson about adaptation or about how characters like Juliet survive across centuries, this might be a gentle way in, though of course that's my suggestion rather than anything in the film's description.

Taken together, these four give you a small ballet evening in miniature. You could begin with the Manon introduction for the story, move to the rehearsal film for the craft, and finish with Lauren Cuthbertson for the human side. None of them is a full performance, and I don't want to suggest otherwise. They are introductions, glimpses and conversations, but they're free and they're well suited to a quiet hour.

Now to ARTE, which is one of your platforms. These three items are on the ARTE Concert channel on YouTube, and they're a more varied bunch.

The one I'd put first is an ARTE Regards reportage called À Valence, sauver les photos de l'inondation. It follows young volunteers who are restoring photographs lost in the floods of October twenty twenty-four in Valence. According to the description, over a million images are still waiting to be saved. The film runs for thirty minutes and, as I understand it, it's available until twenty twenty-seven, so there's no rush. And Valence is not far from you, which gives it a local resonance. I think it's a good-news story in the best sense: not a story where nothing went wrong, but one where people, and young people in particular, have turned up to repair something. Photographs are a kind of memory made physical, and a flood takes away family faces, weddings, holidays, places. There's something close to literature in the idea of rescuing images that hold other people's stories. If you want one piece from today that is warm and human, and a little close to home, I'd choose this.

The second is an episode of the ARTE series PhantasIA, titled La fabrique des émotions artificielles, which is about how artificial intelligence is learning to recognise, imitate and govern human emotions. The range is wide: from acting and neurodivergence, through to psychiatry and facial recognition. It's a subject that sits quite close to what you do, since so much of fiction is about how we read emotion in one another, in a face, a gesture, a tone of voice. An actor's craft is, in a sense, the imitation of feeling, and the programme apparently touches on acting directly. I can't say how it treats the subject or what conclusions it draws, since the description only lists the territory it covers. But it may give you good material for a conversation with older pupils, particularly those approaching the terminale, about what it means to read and to perform emotion.

The third is an ARTE Twist episode called Pourquoi le mignon nous fait du bien, which asks why cute things comfort us. It looks at everything from kawaii culture to Labubu keychains. The description calls it a thoughtful cultural piece that links art, design and the search for reassurance in troubled times. It's a lighter watch than the other two, but I like the idea at its centre: that a small, soft, rounded object can speak to something real in us, particularly when the world feels uncertain. It's the kind of programme that might make you look at a shelf of small figures with fresh eyes. Whether it's a piece you'd enjoy or find a little frivolous, I can't say, but it's presented with some seriousness, and it's French, which makes it convenient material for your pupils as well.

So if I were choosing a short list for you today, it would run something like this. For something to watch tonight, the Manon introduction, which gives you a character and a story in miniature. For something with real heart, the Valence film from ARTE, since it's both local and hopeful. For the weekend, keep an eye out for the Netflix thriller on the thirty-first, and perhaps hunt for the HBO and Harlan Coben series, bearing in mind that I only have headlines for those and can't promise anything about their quality or where they live.

One last note on the limits of what I know. Several of today's items are descriptions rather than reviews, and three of them are headlines alone. So I'd treat the thrillers as leads to follow rather than firm recommendations, and the ballet and ARTE films as the surer bets.

That's your viewing for today, Yamuna. I hope there's a good cup of something warm and a comfortable chair waiting for it.

briefing.text:
Good morning, Yamuna, and happy Friday.

Let me start close to home, because one thing is happening today. At the library in Sainte-Marie-d'Alloix, between eleven o'clock and noon, there's a storytelling show called Kamishibike. It uses kamishibai, the Japanese picture-card theatre, and it's performed by bike. It's a lovely way to step into a story with no preparation at all. Also nearby, in Pontcharra, the arts group Art'M is celebrating its twenty-fifth anniversary with an exhibition, open until the sixth of November, according to Le Dauphiné Libéré. And the same paper says the Mois du film documentaire is coming to the Grésivaudan. It gives no dates or screenings, so the listings will need checking, but it sounds right up your street.

On to books, which are generous this morning. The Guardian reviews Attention Seeking Behaviour by Aea Varfis-van Warmelo, a debut shortlisted for the Goldsmiths Prize. The narrator shares the author's name and confesses, almost at once, that she is a liar. The reviewer sets it beside Lolita and Atonement, and it's a slippery study of memory, justice and truth. Your première classes might enjoy arguing over whether to believe her.

The Guardian also reviews Hanif Kureishi's Are You With Me Now?, written after an accident left him tetraplegic. The reviewer finds that his restricted life has given the narration a new, thrilling immediacy, rebellious and vivid. A novelist unleashed, as the headline puts it.

And a book that joins painting to history: in The New York Times, a review of Joan Martelli's The Widow van Gogh. The biography argues that Vincent's work might never have reached the world without his sister-in-law, Johanna van Gogh-Bonger. It's a story about how a legacy gets made, and how much depends on one person's stubborn devotion.

There's also an interview with the South African novelist Damon Galgut, in the Korean paper Asia Economy. He talks about wishing he could write a love story free from history, and about the questions his fiction leaves open. It touches on how novels carry history whether they mean to or not.

Now to the stage and the gallery. Front Row on BBC Radio 4 has an episode reviewing Nina Raine's six-hour adaptation of Middlemarch for the Royal Shakespeare Company, asking how the stage version compares with George Eliot's novel. The same programme visits the British Library's Agatha Christie exhibition, marking fifty years since her death. A long novel on stage and a queen of crime on the wall: a good half hour for you.

In art, The Guardian is full of praise for William Kentridge's Oh to Believe in Another World, staged in Baku. It's an hour-long collage animation, with a live orchestra playing Shostakovich's Tenth Symphony. The reviewer describes puppetry, dance and humour, all circling grief and idealism, and calls it an amazing animated ballet of black comic pain. It sounds like music, drawing and movement all at once.

A few items for your BFI planning. Everything Theatre has reviewed a production of Twelfth Night at the Crucible Theatre in Sheffield. Twelfth Night is on the list for the twenty twenty-seven session, so a critic's account of a staging could be handy for seconde, première and terminale. I only have the headline, so the detail will be in the review itself. And there is sad news from The Guardian: it reports the death of Sir Patrick Stewart, at eighty-six, remembered as the Star Trek actor and as an acclaimed thespian. For someone who loves the theatre, it's a name that carries a great deal of Shakespeare with it.

For something to watch, the Royal Ballet and Opera has two short videos on YouTube. One is an introduction to Kenneth MacMillan's Manon, the devastating ballet set in eighteenth-century Paris about a woman torn between love and wealth. The other, for World Ballet Day, shows dancers in rehearsal preparing Visionaries: Robbins and MacMillan for the main stage. Both are free, and both are good company with a cup of tea.

Now to some good news. Positive News reports from Namibia, where rangers are combining smartphones and real-time data with ancient tracking skills. They are helping farmers and protecting a recovering population of desert lions. It's a pleasing picture of local knowledge working alongside modern tools rather than being replaced by them.

And from Good News Network, research suggests that birdwatching may rewire the brain. The expertise needed to identify birds seems to help preserve neuroplasticity, and may slow cognitive decline in later life. The article opens with Emily Dickinson's line about hope being the thing with feathers, which seems just right for an autumn walk above the valley.

Finally, two stories from France. The Guardian reports that a cache of rare love letters, written by La Pérouse, has come to light. He was the scientist lost on Louis XVI's round-the-world voyage that set out in seventeen eighty-five. The letters give a personal account of the expedition, and it sounds like a novel waiting to be written. Lastly, The Local France says it has found the town where people speak the most perfect French. The report is slim on detail, but the question of what counts as standard French, and who gets to decide, is one a language teacher might enjoy turning over.

That's your Friday, Yamuna. I hope your day has a good story in it, and a bit of sunshine over Belledonne.
